mastery.oneLine: Neck and spine glides applied along the facet joint while the patient moves actively (SNAG) or in gentle oscillation (NAG).
mastery.whatItIs: SNAG means Sustained Natural Apophyseal Glide: you glide one vertebra along the angle of its facet joint while the patient actively moves the painful way. NAG means Natural Apophyseal Glide, applied as a gentle oscillating glide, often to find the right direction. Self-SNAGs let the patient apply the glide themselves with a towel or hands.
mastery.analogy: A facet joint is like a ramp. If you push the vertebra up the ramp's own slope while the neck turns, the movement runs smoothly; if you push across it, the movement jams.
coreIdeas: Glide along the facet plane, roughly toward the patient's eyes in the neck, while the patient moves.
The movement must be pain-free and clearly better at once (the same PILL idea as other Mulligan techniques).
Because it is near the neck, careful screening for blood-vessel and neurological problems comes first.

terms.meaning: Another name for the facet joint, the small paired joints at the back of each vertebra.
A held glide with the patient moving through it.
A version where the patient holds a towel or their fingers on the vertebra and applies the glide themselves.
Dizziness, nausea, visual change or numbness mean stop immediately.

whenToUse: Painful neck rotation or flexion where a segment is tender.
Headaches arising from the upper neck that are reproduced by neck movement.
whenNot: Dizziness, visual disturbance, difficulty speaking or swallowing, or any neurological sign.
Fracture, instability, infection or unexplained severe pain.

steps.title: Screen for neck red flags
steps.detail: Check for dizziness, visual change, previous neck injury, and neurological symptoms.

steps.title: Find the painful movement
steps.detail: Example: right rotation is painful at 40 degrees.

steps.title: Contact the vertebra
steps.detail: In sitting, place your thumb pads on the side of the painful vertebra's joint, with support behind your thumb.

steps.title: Apply the glide
steps.detail: Glide gently along the facet plane toward the patient's eyes.

steps.title: Ask the patient to move
steps.detail: They turn through the previously painful range while you hold the glide. It should feel easy and pain-free.

steps.title: Repeat and retest
steps.detail: Repeat 6-10 times. Retest rotation. Teach a self-SNAG if effective.

mastery.dose: Typical teaching range: 6-10 repetitions, 2-3 sets. Stay pain-free. Stop if no instant improvement.

example.patient: David, 50, desk worker, neck pain turning to the left to check traffic.
example.assessment: Left rotation is painful at 45 degrees. Screening is clear.
example.treatment: You apply a SNAG at the left C5-6 facet while he turns slowly left. The movement becomes pain-free through the range, so he repeats 8 times, three sets.
example.reassess: Rotation reaches 65 degrees with minimal pain. You teach a towel self-SNAG for home and review in a week.

mistakes: Pushing straight forward instead of along the facet plane.
Continuing when pain does not drop.

selfTest.q: In which direction is the cervical SNAG glide applied?
selfTest.a: Along the facet plane, roughly toward the patient's eyes.

selfTest.q: The patient feels dizzy. What do you do?
selfTest.a: Stop immediately and reassess for safety.

mastery.recap: Glide along the facet, move the neck, and keep it pain-free.
mastery.evidence: Small studies suggest short-term improvement in neck pain and headache, but evidence is limited and the effect over time is uncertain.

depth.why: SNAGs (sustained natural apophyseal glides) apply a sustained glide to the facet joint while the patient actively moves in the painful direction in a weight-bearing position; NAGs are oscillatory glides at the end of range. The method is a mobilisation-with-movement for the spine, with the same instant-effect rule.
choose: Use when a specific spinal movement is painful and a facet glide makes it pain-free at once.
Prefer SNAGs over HVLA when thrust is contraindicated or the patient prefers a gentle method.
Stop and reassess the segment if dizziness, nausea or visual symptoms occur (neck).
parameters: sustained along the facet plane, about 45 degrees toward the eyes for the cervical spine
sitting or standing, weight-bearing, the patient moves actively
daily self-SNAG with a towel or a belt when taught well
depth.progress: Move from pain-free range to end-range overpressure, then to loaded and functional movements. If the movement stays pain-free, fade the glide and have the patient repeat it alone, with a belt or self-SNAG, before adding load.
measure: Pain and range of the target movement
Dizziness or other symptoms during the technique
Function (for example turning to check a blind spot)
depth.evidence: Cervicogenic headache and neck pain trials show benefit in short and medium term, but the studies are small and often not blinded. Safety screening is essential in the neck.
pitfalls: Skipping screening of the neck for vascular and instability signs.
Sliding the skin over the segment instead of gliding the vertebra.
Treating a segment that is not the symptomatic one.
screen: Positive cervical artery screening, dizziness or drop attacks
Acute disc with progressive neurological deficit

heading.en: SNAG, NAG and self-SNAG, one by one
heading.ur: SNAG, NAG aur self-SNAG, ek ek karke

intro.en: All three glide a spinal facet along its own plane. The difference is whether the patient moves actively, and who does the work.
intro.ur: Teeno spinal facet ko uske apne plane par glide karte hain. Farq yeh hai ke patient active move karta hai ya nahi, aur kaam kaun karta hai.

tag.en: Sustained glide while the patient moves
tag.ur: Patient ke hilte waqt sustained glide

what.en: A sustained glide along the facet while the patient actively makes the painful or stiff movement. It must be pain-free.
what.ur: Facet ke saath sustained glide jabke patient active taur par dardnak ya akri hui movement karta hai. Pain-free hona zaroori hai.

en: Find the level and the facet plane.
Hold the glide with the thumb or a belt.
Ask the patient to make the movement and repeat 6 to 10 times.
ur: Thumb ya belt se glide hold karein.
Patient se movement karwayein aur 6 se 10 dafa dohrayein.

watch.en: Stop for dizziness, nausea or pain.
watch.ur: Chakkar, matli ya dard par rukein.

what.en: A gentle rhythmic glide along the facet with the patient sitting and relaxed, usually in the neck and upper back.
what.ur: Facet ke saath narm rhythmic glide jabke patient baitha aur relaxed ho, aam taur par gardan aur upar ki peeth mein.

en: Apply the glide with the thumbs on the facet.
Oscillate gently for a few repetitions and retest.
ur: Thumbs se facet par glide dein.
Chand dafa narmi se oscillate karein aur retest karein.

watch.en: Check dizziness and neurological signs first.
watch.ur: Pehle chakkar aur neurological signs check karein.

what.en: The patient applies the glide with a towel, strap or hand and moves actively, as home practice once the clinician has shown the technique.
what.ur: Patient towel, strap ya haath se glide lagata hai aur active move karta hai, ghar ki practice ke taur par jab clinician technique dikha chuka ho.

en: Learn the exact position with the therapist.
Apply the glide with the strap or hand.
Move actively, a few repetitions, only if pain-free.
ur: Therapist ke saath durust position seekhein.
Strap ya haath se glide lagayein.
Active move karein, chand dafa, sirf agar pain-free ho.

urdu.short: NAGs, SNAGs aur Self-SNAGs spinal mobilization ke tareeqay hain jin mein joint ki glide ko passive ya active movement ke sath combine kiya jata hai. Asal maqsad comfortable movement aur patient ke response ko dekhna hai.

details.heading: Summary — khulasa
details.text: Yeh techniques spinal facet joints ki direction mein glide ko movement ke sath combine karti hain. Self-SNAG mein patient ko safe tareeqay se khud movement karna sikhaya ja sakta hai.

details.heading: Science — source kya kehta hai
details.text: In ka maqsad patient ki participation ke sath pain-free spinal movement behtar karna hai. Self-SNAG safe tareeqay se sikhaya jaye to manual concept ko home strategy mein badal sakta hai. Response ko foran movement ki tabdeeli aur symptoms ke rawaiye se judge karna chahiye.

details.heading: Procedure — tareeqa
details.text:
1. Limited spinal movement identify karein.
2. Mutaliqa segment par intended direction mein glide dein.
3. SNAG mein glide maintain karte hue patient se active movement karwayein.
4. Sirf us surat mein repeat karein jab movement comfortable rahe aur behtari ho.
5. Self-SNAG tabhi sikhayein jab patient direction ko mehfooz tareeqay se dohra sake.

details.heading: Dosage — miqdaar
details.text: Aksar ek set mein 6–10 repetitions istemal ki jati hain, lekin sets ki tadaad response ke mutabiq hoti hai. Home self-SNAG ki dose conservative aur symptoms ke mutabiq honi chahiye.

details.heading: Indications — source mein di gayi surat-e-haal
details.text: Mechanical spinal pain; dard ke sath movement restriction; screening ke baad kuch selected headache ya cervicogenic presentations.

details.heading: Precautions — ehtiyati baatein
details.text: Upper cervical symptoms, chakkar, ya vascular ya ligament-related disorder ki history ho to khaas ehtiyat aur munasib screening zaroori hai.

details.heading: Contraindications — kab na karein
details.text: Cervical arterial pathology ka shak, instability, fracture, acute myelopathy, ya barhta hua neurological deficit.

details.heading: Reassessment — dobara jaanch
details.text: Pain-free spinal range, functional movement, aur zaroorat par headache ya doosray symptoms ka response dobara check karein.

details.heading: Pearl — yaad rakhne wali baat
details.text: Cervical technique se pehle munasib vascular, neurological aur ligament-related screening zaroori hai.

details.heading: Misal — sirf samjhane ke liye
details.text: Farz karein neck ghumane mein takleef hai. Assessment aur screening ke baad therapist glide ke sath movement ka response check karta hai. Agar movement comfortable na ho, to technique ko force nahi karta. Yeh fictional example hai, patient-specific prescription nahi.

deeper.heading: NAGs aur SNAGs ka farq
deeper.text: NAGs aam tor par spinal joint par therapist ki oscillatory glide approach ko kehte hain, jabke SNAG mein glide ke saath patient ki active movement hoti hai. Dono ko aik hi cheez na samjhein. Selection symptoms, movement assessment, anatomical region aur trained clinical judgement par depend karti hai.

deeper.heading: Clinical application
deeper.text: Relevant movement aur symptoms ka baseline record karein. Patient ko comfortable position dein aur glide ko controlled direction mein apply karein. SNAG mein active movement glide ke saath coordinate hoti hai aur comfortable rehni chahiye. Spine, khaas taur par neck, par application se pehle safety screening aur supervised competency zaroori hai.

deeper.heading: Common mistakes aur safety
deeper.text: Technique ka naam yaad hona safe application ke barabar nahi. Movement force karna, feedback ignore karna, unsuitable presentation mein use karna aur retest skip karna aam ghaltiyan hain. Dizziness, nayi neurological symptoms, unusual severe pain ya worsening symptoms hon to rok kar appropriate assessment karein.

deeper.heading: Outcome aur evidence
deeper.text: Sirf therapist ke hand ke neeche joint feel ko outcome na banayein. Patient ki active movement, symptoms aur function compare karein. Isay guaranteed long-term structural change ke taur par present na karein; English chapter ki evidence summary ke mutabiq balanced explanation dein.

cue.wake: Necks are not steering wheels. No sudden turns to win a race!
cue.question: During a cervical SNAG, who should actively turn the head?
cue.answer: The patient, in a screened and comfortable range. The clinician controls the selected contact.
cue.easy: SNAG = a sustained accessory glide paired with an active movement.
cue.remember: Patient moves; therapist guides; safety decides.

technique.storyHeadline: A painful neck movement. A different way to explore it.

episode.patient: A teacher turns to face a student at the back of the classroom and gets an unwelcome reminder from the neck. The familiar painful rotation becomes a measurable starting point, but cervical screening comes before any clever technique.
episode.decision: Depending on the presentation and training, you consider an appropriate NAG or SNAG. Contact, direction and timing matter, and any assisted active movement should remain comfortable. The neck is not a steering wheel you force into a turn.
episode.retest: When your hands leave, the teacher turns again. You look for a meaningful change in symptoms or range, while remaining alert for any unusual headache, dizziness, visual or neurological symptoms that require stopping and assessment.
episode.spark: A smoother head turn beats an impressive-looking maneuver every time.

aha.hook: Your hand is not a steering wheel for the patient's neck.
aha.analogy: With a carefully selected SNAG, the patient remains an active driver of the movement. Your role is to guide the trial safely, not to force the turn farther than their symptoms allow.
aha.challenge: A cervical glide produces dizziness and an unusual headache. Is that just part of finding the right angle?
aha.reveal: No. Stop, assess the symptoms appropriately and do not continue manual treatment through concerning signs.

weave.dialogue: Patient: 'I need to turn my head to drive, not audition for a circus trick.' Clinician: 'Excellent. We'll test the actual movement, and comfort comes before range.'
weave.watch: Picture a seated patient, feet supported, eyes level. The practitioner chooses a trained, precise cervical contact. During an appropriate SNAG, the patient—not the therapist—performs the head turn. The task stops before unusual symptoms or painful forcing begin.
weave.method: This is guidance, not a steering wheel attached to someone else's neck. Keep the line of force controlled, check the symptom response immediately, and never let a smoother-looking movement hide concerning dizziness, headache or neurological changes.
weave.science: A short-term improvement in neck movement may reflect several interacting processes. It is not a camera view of a facet joint being 'pushed back' into a normal place.
weave.question: The patient reports sudden dizziness during the glide, even though rotation increased. Does the extra range make the technique successful?
weave.answer: No. Stop and assess the unexpected symptom appropriately; consider cervical vascular and neurological screening. A range gain never overrules safety.
weave.closer: The patient owns the neck turn; the therapist owns the responsibility to stop.

patientPosition: For cervical or thoracic work, sitting often allows the patient to actively reproduce the restricted movement while you guide the segment.
Keep the patient upright and relaxed, with feet supported when possible.
therapistPosition: Stand slightly behind or beside the patient so your hands can contact the selected vertebral level without forcing your own wrists.
Your body should follow the plane of the facet glide rather than pushing straight into the spine.
handPlacement: Use a comfortable contact over the articular pillar or spinous process depending on the technique and region.
A towel or belt can be used for self-SNAG teaching when appropriate.
Avoid pressure over the anterior neck, carotid region or painful superficial structures.
forceDirection: NAGs use a gentle oscillatory glide in the relevant facet plane.
SNAGs use a sustained segmental glide while the patient actively performs the restricted movement.
The force should assist the movement rather than jam the joint or create pain.
applicationSteps: 1. Screen cervical neurological and vascular concerns before cervical manual therapy.
3. Select the suspected level and apply a low-force glide in the facet plane.
4. For a SNAG, maintain the glide while the patient slowly performs the movement.
5. If pain persists, modify level, angle or force. Do not force through pain.
6. Repeat only when the movement becomes easier or pain-free.
7. Retest without your hands. If useful, teach a safe self-SNAG and pair it with active control/strength.
expectedResponse: Immediate improvement in pain-free spinal motion or a meaningful functional task.
stopCriteria: Dizziness, visual disturbance, unusual headache, neurological change, nausea, drop attacks, severe pain or any symptom that raises vascular/neurological concern.
commonMistakes: Using a generic posterior push rather than following the facet plane.
Teaching a self-SNAG before the patient can reproduce the correct direction safely.
clinicalExample: Example: limited pain-free cervical rotation. Apply a carefully selected SNAG while the patient turns. If rotation improves, reinforce with active rotation and cervical/scapular endurance work.

mechanism.mechanismMap: Segmental glide + spinal movement → altered afferent input + pain-free motor experience → reduced guarding + improved spinal motion
mechanism.simpleExplanation: NAGs and SNAGs expose the spine to a comfortable segmental glide while movement occurs. The combination can change sensory input from the joint and surrounding tissues, reduce pain sensitivity and let the patient experience the movement with less threat and less muscle guarding.
stepByStep: 1. A restricted or painful spinal movement is identified.
2. A segmental glide changes local mechanical input.
3. During a SNAG, the patient actively performs the movement at the same time.
4. The nervous system receives a different pattern of joint, muscle and skin input.
5. If pain reduces, protective muscle activity can decrease and motion can increase.
7. Self-SNAGs can extend the same sensory-motor strategy into self-management.
physiology: Segmental mechanoreceptor stimulation can modify spinal nociceptive processing.
Active movement recruits cortical motor and sensorimotor networks.
Descending modulation can contribute to short-term analgesia.
Reduced pain may permit a larger active range without needing a large structural change.
The exact vertebral segment selected clinically may not be the only structure producing the response.
clinicalTranslation: A good SNAG should make the comparable movement easier or pain-free.
If the response is not immediate, reconsider level, direction, force or diagnosis.
Carry-over should be reinforced with active control and endurance.
myths: Do not claim that a specific vertebra is permanently realigned.
Do not use pain during the technique as proof that the 'right level' has been found.
mechanism.evidenceNote: The most plausible explanation is a combined mechanical, neurophysiological and sensorimotor effect rather than a simple positional correction.

mechanismEvidence.summary: Manual therapy does not have one universal mechanism. Modern evidence supports interacting peripheral, spinal, supraspinal, neurovascular, neuromuscular and contextual responses. The exact mechanism responsible for a patient's clinical improvement is often uncertain.
mechanismEvidence.sourceTitle: The mechanisms of manual therapy: A living review of systematic, narrative, and scoping reviews

room.arrival: The patient imagines checking traffic over their shoulder and pauses at a familiar neck pain. You review the history and screen concerning neurological or vascular features first.
room.touch: In suitably trained hands, a carefully directed NAG or SNAG may be trialed. With a SNAG, the patient performs the active movement; you do not steer the neck through pain.
room.retest: Retest rotation without assistance. Any new dizziness, unusual headache, visual symptoms or neurological change means stop and assess—not 'find a better angle.'
